questions.stem: A 44 year old accountant has had headaches on most afternoons during the 6 weeks of year-end. She describes a pressure 'like a hat that is too tight' over both sides of her head. The pain is mild to moderate and she keeps working. She has no nausea or visual symptoms. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Her neck and shoulder muscles are tender and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral, tight, mild to moderate pain linked to stress, with tender pericranial muscles and a normal neurological exam, is tension-type headache. Migraine is typically unilateral, throbbing and with nausea.

clues: over both sides of her head
Her neck and shoulder muscles are tender
steps.x: Bilateral band-like pressure, mild to moderate severity, a stress trigger and muscle tenderness with a normal neuro exam.

elim: Unilateral orbital pain with tearing and restlessness, not bilateral pressure.
She is not described as taking frequent analgesia.
Usually unilateral, throbbing, with nausea and worse with activity.
Age over 50, scalp tenderness over the artery and jaw claudication; she is 44.

steps.x: E: Tension-type headache. Bilateral, pressing, band-like and mild to moderate = tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 34 year old male teacher has a 2 month history of headaches at the end of most school days. He describes a dull, tight band around his head that is eased by rest and a walk. He has no vomiting or weakness. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. You are about to examine him.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
o: Neck stiffness with a positive Kernig sign
questions.e: Tension-type headache is a clinical diagnosis with a normal neurological examination; only scalp and neck muscle tenderness may be found. Any focal sign or papilloedema points to a secondary cause.

clues: dull, tight band around his head
eased by rest and a walk
steps.x: A typical tension-type picture with no red flags.

elim: Suggests raised intracranial pressure, which would be a red flag, not tension-type headache.
Horner's pattern is seen in cluster headache or carotid dissection.
Meningism is a red flag for meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage.
A focal deficit is a red flag for a structural cause.

steps.x: D: No abnormal neurological findings. In tension-type headache the neuro exam is normal; abnormal signs mean look for another cause.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has had tension-type headaches for years, eased by ibuprofen. He asks his GP which changes in his headaches should make him seek emergency help. He works as a builder and his headaches are worse on stressful days. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which new feature would most warrant emergency assessment?
o: Headache after a poor night's sleep
Sudden severe headache peaking within a minute
Tender neck muscles at the end of the day
questions.e: A sudden, severe (thunderclap) headache is an emergency red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage. The other features are typical of tension-type headache.

clues: which changes in his headaches should make him seek emergency help
steps.x: The question asks for a red flag, not a typical feature.

elim: A typical trigger of tension-type headache, not a red flag.
Response to simple analgesia is expected in tension-type headache.
This is the usual character of tension-type headache.
Pericranial muscle tenderness is part of tension-type headache.

steps.x: D: Sudden severe headache peaking within a minute. Red flags: sudden severe headache, neurological signs, or meningism.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man had episodic migraines and tension-type headaches. For the past 4 months he has had a headache on most days, often present on waking. He takes sumatriptan on about 15 days each month and paracetamol on others. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 126/82 mmHg. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Daily headache, often on waking, in someone taking triptans and analgesics on most days is medication overuse headache. A normal fundoscopy argues against idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

clues: headache on most days, often present on waking
sumatriptan on about 15 days each month
steps.x: Pre-existing headache that has become daily alongside frequent triptan and analgesic use.

elim: No aura is described and the change follows frequent medication use.
Short unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic features.
Fundoscopy is normal, with no papilloedema.
No head injury, anticoagulation or neurological signs.

steps.x: D: Medication overuse headache. Frequent analgesic or triptan use turning episodic headache into daily headache = medication overuse headache.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had near-daily headaches while taking paracetamol and ibuprofen on most days for 6 months. She stopped all analgesia 6 weeks ago. Her headaches were worse for the first week but have now returned to her old pattern of mild bilateral pressing headaches twice a month. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. Her headache diary is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Headache days per month
visual.caption: Near-daily headache falls back to her baseline of about 2 days a month after stopping analgesia.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis of her near-daily headaches?
questions.e: Reverting to the original headache pattern within 2 months of stopping the overused medication confirms medication overuse headache.

steps.x: Resolution back to the baseline pattern within 2 months of withdrawal.

elim: Would not revert to an episodic pattern simply on stopping analgesia.
Daily headache that resolves on stopping analgesia is caused by the medication.
Starts abruptly and persists; it does not resolve on stopping analgesia.
Causes liver injury, not a headache pattern.

steps.x: C: Medication overuse headache. Revert within 2 months of stopping the drug = medication overuse headache confirmed.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with tension-type headache has had daily headaches for 3 months while taking paracetamol and ibuprofen most days. His GP suspects medication overuse headache and he agrees to stop all analgesics. His BP is 132/84 mmHg and neurological examination is normal. He asks how the diagnosis will be confirmed.
questions.q: Within which period must the headache resolve, or revert to its earlier pattern, to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Medication overuse headache is diagnosed when symptoms resolve, or revert to the original pattern, within 2 months of stopping the causative medication, reflecting slow normalisation of central pain pathways.

clues: how the diagnosis will be confirmed
steps.x: The question asks for the diagnostic time window after withdrawal.

elim: Too long; the criterion is 2 months.
Far too short; pain pathways take weeks to normalise.
Too short; many patients are still improving at 2 weeks.
Too long; the criterion is 2 months.

steps.x: C: 2 months. Medication overuse headache: improvement within 2 months of stopping confirms it.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 3 month history of headaches 2 or 3 times a week. The pain is a bilateral pressure across her forehead, lasting several hours. She still goes for her evening run and the headache is no worse afterwards. She has no nausea. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which feature most favours tension-type headache over migraine?
o: Headache not worsened by physical activity
questions.e: Migraine is typically aggravated by routine physical activity; tension-type headache is not. Duration, sex and a normal examination do not separate the two.

steps.x: Running does not worsen the pain, and it is bilateral with no nausea.

elim: Both migraine and tension-type headache can last hours.
Both conditions are more common in women.
Also expected between and during most migraines.
Both commonly start in young adults.

steps.x: C: Headache not worsened by physical activity. Not aggravated by routine activity points to tension-type headache, not migraine.

questions.stem: A 22 year old student has had bilateral pressing headaches for 4 weeks during her final exams. She revises until 3am, sleeps about 5 hours, skips lunch and drinks little water. The pain is mild and she can carry on studying. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Visual acuity, fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her headaches?
questions.e: Stress, poor sleep, dehydration and missed meals increase pericranial muscle tension and trigger tension-type headache. The normal examination excludes the structural causes.

clues: skips lunch and drinks little water
steps.x: Exam stress, sleep loss, dehydration and missed meals with a normal examination.

elim: No red flags: examination and fundoscopy are normal.
Fundoscopy is normal and there is no vomiting or visual change.
Visual acuity is normal.
No facial pain, fever or nasal symptoms.

steps.x: E: Stress and poor sleep. Stress, fatigue, poor sleep and dehydration trigger tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 33 year old male courier has had headaches on about 10 days a month for a year. He describes a mild to moderate pressing tightness over his scalp and the back of his neck. He has no visual disturbance. His BMI is 24 kg/m². His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows sharp optic discs and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mild to moderate pressing tightness of the scalp and neck with a normal examination is tension-type headache. Sharp optic discs argue against idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

clues: scalp and the back of his neck
steps.x: Mild to moderate pressure with scalp and neck tightness, normal fundi and exam.

elim: Unilateral severe orbital pain with tearing, not a mild pressing tightness.
Usually an obese young woman with papilloedema; his discs are sharp.
No aura or visual disturbance.
Sudden severe headache, not a year of mild recurrent pain.

steps.x: E: Tension-type headache. Mild to moderate pressing scalp/neck tightness = tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl has had headaches for 2 months since starting a new school. She describes a tight squeezing feeling over both sides of her head, worse late in the school day. She is sleeping badly and worries about friendships. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. Visual acuity, fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral squeezing pain linked to stress and poor sleep with a normal examination is tension-type headache. A normal acuity and fundoscopy argue against refractive error and raised pressure.

clues: tight squeezing feeling over both sides of her head
sleeping badly and worries about friendships
fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Bilateral squeeze, stress and poor sleep, normal fundi and exam.

elim: No early morning vomiting, papilloedema or neurological signs.
No aura, nausea or unilateral throbbing pain.
Visual acuity is normal.
No fever, facial pain or nasal discharge.

steps.x: E: Tension-type headache. Band-like bilateral pressure with stress and a normal exam = tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 38 year old female call centre worker has a 3 month history of bilateral pressing headaches that build during her shifts at a computer. She has no nausea, photophobia or weakness. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Reduced eye movements on lateral gaze
questions.e: Tension-type headache has a normal neurological exam with tenderness of the scalp and neck/shoulder muscles, reflecting the peripheral myofascial component.

clues: Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Posture-related bilateral pressing pain with a normal neuro exam.

elim: Meningism is a red flag, not a feature of tension-type headache.
Suggests temporal arteritis in older patients.
A cranial nerve palsy is a red flag for a secondary cause.
Autonomic features suggest cluster headache.

steps.x: D: Tender trapezius and neck muscles. Expect pericranial and neck/shoulder muscle tenderness in tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has a 4 month history of bilateral pressing headaches at the end of stressful working days. They are mild and ease with paracetamol, which he takes about twice a week. He is anxious and asks for a brain scan. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: No investigation; the diagnosis is clinical
questions.e: Tension-type headache is a clinical diagnosis; with a typical history, infrequent analgesia and a normal examination, no imaging is needed. Reassurance is part of management.

clues: Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Typical history, no red flags, normal exam: the scan request does not change that.

elim: Imaging is not needed without red flags and does not confirm tension-type headache.
Used for suspected temporal arteritis in patients over 50.
For suspected meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage; no meningism or thunderclap onset.
Not indicated without red flags, even if the patient asks.

steps.x: E: No investigation; the diagnosis is clinical. Tension-type headache: clinical diagnosis, no routine imaging.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has had headaches on and off for a year. Some are bilateral and pressing, others she cannot describe well. She is unsure how often they occur, what sets them off, or how many tablets she takes. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A headache diary records frequency, triggers and medication use, which helps classify recurrent headache and spot medication overuse. Imaging is not indicated without red flags.

clues: unsure how often they occur, what sets them off, or how many tablets she takes
Fundoscopy and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: The gaps are frequency, triggers and tablet use, with a normal examination.

elim: No red flags; imaging will not clarify frequency or triggers.
Will not characterise a primary headache.
No red flags; not a first-line test.
Not relevant to recurrent headache.

steps.x: C: Headache diary. Recurrent headache with an unclear pattern: start a headache diary.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has had tension-type headaches for 10 years. Over 3 weeks her headaches have changed: they are worse on waking, she has vomited twice and she has noticed clumsiness of her left hand. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 64 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. She has pronator drift of the left arm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: A headache with new neurological signs is a red flag and needs urgent investigation for a secondary cause such as a tumour. Known tension-type headache does not explain a focal deficit.

clues: worse on waking, she has vomited twice
pronator drift of the left arm
steps.x: A change in pattern with morning vomiting and a focal deficit.

elim: Delays urgent assessment of a red-flag headache.
A new neurological deficit cannot be attributed to tension-type headache.
Prophylaxis is not appropriate before a secondary cause is excluded.
Medication overuse does not cause focal neurological signs.

steps.x: D: Urgent brain imaging. Red flag present: investigate urgently for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with long-standing tension-type headache now has headaches on most days. He kept a headache diary for 8 weeks at his GP's request. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. The GP suspects his daily headaches are caused by his treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding in his headache diary?
o: Analgesics taken on most days of the month
Attacks clustered in the same few weeks each year
questions.e: A diary in medication overuse headache shows analgesic use on most days of the month, which is how the diary identifies overuse as well as triggers and frequency.

steps.x: Daily headache in someone with tension-type headache, with treatment suspected as the cause.

elim: Seasonal clusters suggest cluster headache.
Suggests a dietary or alcohol trigger, not overuse of treatment.
Suggests caffeine withdrawal, not overuse of treatment.
Suggests trigeminal neuralgia or temporomandibular disorder.

steps.x: A: Analgesics taken on most days of the month. The diary exposes medication overuse: analgesia on most days.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with known tension-type headache attends the emergency department with a severe headache for 1 day. He has vomited and dislikes bright light. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. He has neck stiffness and pain on neck flexion.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure that this is his usual headache
Urgent investigation for a secondary cause
questions.e: Headache with meningism is an emergency red flag; he needs urgent assessment (bloods, cultures, imaging and lumbar puncture as appropriate) for meningitis or haemorrhage.

clues: neck stiffness and pain on neck flexion
steps.x: Fever, photophobia and meningism in someone with a history of benign headache.

elim: Fever and meningism must not be treated as a tension-type headache.
Far too slow for possible meningitis.
Treats migraine; this is a red-flag headache.
Fever and neck stiffness are not features of tension-type headache.

steps.x: E: Urgent investigation for a secondary cause. Meningism is a red flag: investigate urgently for a secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has tension-type headaches about 3 times a month, each lasting a few hours. He had a bleeding duodenal ulcer last year. He has tried nothing yet. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal and he has tender neck muscles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Simple analgesia is first line for tension-type headache; paracetamol is the safer choice after a bleeding ulcer. Opioids and triptans are not recommended.

clues: tension-type headaches about 3 times a month
steps.x: First-line simple analgesia, but an NSAID contraindication.

elim: NSAIDs are best avoided after a bleeding peptic ulcer.
Opioids are not recommended for tension-type headache and risk overuse headache.
Daily NSAID use risks ulcer bleeding and medication overuse.
Triptans treat migraine, not tension-type headache.

steps.x: A: As-needed paracetamol. Tension-type headache: simple analgesia first line, chosen around comorbidity.

questions.stem: A 26 year old junior doctor has tension-type headaches after night shifts. She drinks little during shifts, often misses meals and sleeps poorly. Paracetamol helps but she wants to rely on tablets less. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
o: Hydration, regular meals, sleep and stress reduction
Sumatriptan at the start of each headache
questions.e: Lifestyle and trigger management (sleep, hydration, regular meals and stress reduction) is first line alongside simple analgesia in tension-type headache.

clues: drinks little during shifts, often misses meals and sleeps poorly
steps.x: Obvious modifiable triggers and a wish to cut medication.

elim: A migraine prophylactic; not first choice for episodic tension-type headache.
No red flags; imaging is not part of management.
Opioids risk medication overuse headache.
Triptans treat migraine, not tension-type headache.

steps.x: B: Hydration, regular meals, sleep and stress reduction. Treat the triggers: sleep, hydration, meals and stress.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has been diagnosed with tension-type headache. He has headaches about 6 days a month during busy periods at work. He plans to take ibuprofen and paracetamol together every day 'to keep the headaches away'. His BP is 120/78 mmHg and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about his analgesia?
o: Avoid frequent use; take them only on headache days
Take both every day as prevention
questions.e: Simple analgesia is first line, but frequent use can cause medication overuse headache, so it should be taken only when needed and not on most days.

clues: every day 'to keep the headaches away'
steps.x: He plans to take daily analgesia for an intermittent headache.

elim: Opioids are not recommended and carry the highest overuse risk.
Daily analgesia causes medication overuse headache.
Still daily analgesic use, with the same overuse risk.
Triptans treat migraine and can also cause overuse headache.

steps.x: B: Avoid frequent use; take them only on headache days. Use analgesia when needed; frequent use causes medication overuse headache.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has medication overuse headache. She has taken ibuprofen on about 20 days a month for 5 months for tension-type headache. She takes no other medication. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and neurological examination is normal. She is willing to change her treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reduce ibuprofen by one tablet each week
questions.e: In medication overuse headache all overused medication is stopped; simple analgesics and triptans are stopped abruptly, whereas opioids are withdrawn gradually.

clues: ibuprofen on about 20 days a month
steps.x: The overused drug is a simple analgesic only.

elim: The overused drug must be stopped.
Simple analgesics should be stopped abruptly, not tapered.
Swaps one overused drug for another with even greater risk.
Triptans also cause overuse headache.

steps.x: C: Stop ibuprofen abruptly. Simple analgesics and triptans: stop abruptly.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has medication overuse headache. He has taken dihydrocodeine 30 mg three times a day for 7 months for tension-type headache that became daily. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal. He agrees to stop it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to stop his medication?
questions.e: All overused medication is stopped, but opioids such as codeine and dihydrocodeine are withdrawn gradually to avoid withdrawal, unlike simple analgesics and triptans which are stopped abruptly.

clues: dihydrocodeine 30 mg three times a day for 7 months
steps.x: The overused drug is an opioid.

elim: The overused medication must be stopped.
Abrupt opioid withdrawal risks withdrawal symptoms; opioids are tapered.
Triptans also cause medication overuse headache.
Another opioid that perpetuates overuse headache.

steps.x: E: Withdraw dihydrocodeine gradually. Opioids in medication overuse headache: withdraw gradually.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman stopped paracetamol and sumatriptan 2 weeks ago for medication overuse headache. Her headaches were worse in the first few days and are still present on most days. She asks whether to restart her tablets. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue without them; improvement is expected within about a month
Diagnosis is wrong as she has not improved at 2 weeks
questions.e: Stopping the causative medication should improve the headache within about a month as central pain pathways normalise; full resolution may take up to 2 months.

clues: stopped paracetamol and sumatriptan 2 weeks ago
steps.x: Only 2 weeks after withdrawal, still struggling.

elim: Improvement can take weeks; the criterion allows up to 2 months.
Restarting the overused drug perpetuates the headache.
Triptans also perpetuate overuse headache.
Opioids cause overuse headache too.

steps.x: A: Continue without them; improvement is expected within about a month. Expect improvement within about 1 month of stopping; do not restart.

questions.stem: A 43 year old software developer has bilateral band-like headaches that build through the working day. He sits hunched at a laptop for 10 hours, drinks little water and sleeps 5 hours a night. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. His neck and shoulder muscles are tender. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism linking his lifestyle to his headaches?
questions.e: Poor posture, dehydration and sleep disturbance increase pericranial muscle tension, contributing to the bilateral band-like pain of tension-type headache.

clues: drinks little water and sleeps 5 hours
neck and shoulder muscles are tender
steps.x: Posture, dehydration and poor sleep with tender pericranial muscles.

elim: The mechanism of migraine aura.
Underlies cluster headache.
Causes headache with papilloedema, not posture-related pain.
A migraine mechanism; tension-type headache lacks a significant vascular component.

steps.x: C: Increased pericranial muscle tension. Stress, posture, dehydration, poor sleep: raised pericranial muscle tension.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has migraines with throbbing unilateral pain and nausea, and separately bilateral pressing headaches during stressful weeks. A medical student asks how the two headaches differ in mechanism. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which mechanism is a feature of migraine but not of her pressing headaches?
questions.e: Tension-type headache has no significant vascular or trigeminal-autonomic component; trigeminovascular activation is the hallmark of migraine.

clues: bilateral pressing headaches during stressful weeks
steps.x: Two headache types; find the mechanism unique to migraine.

elim: Also contributes to tension-type headache.
The peripheral component of tension-type headache.
Triggers both conditions.
Triggers both conditions.

steps.x: E: Trigeminovascular activation. Tension-type headache: no significant vascular or trigeminal-autonomic component.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with medication overuse headache stops his sumatriptan and paracetamol. His headaches gradually lessen over the following 6 weeks, back to his previous pattern of occasional tension-type headaches. His BP is 128/80 mmHg and neurological examination is normal. He asks why it took so long.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the slow improvement?
o: Clearance of drug from fat stores
Gradual normalisation of central pain pathways
questions.e: Withdrawal allows central pain modulation, downregulated by frequent analgesic use, to normalise over several weeks, which explains the 1 to 2 month resolution time.

clues: gradually lessen over the following 6 weeks
steps.x: The drugs are gone in days, yet improvement takes weeks.

elim: Paracetamol and sumatriptan are cleared within days.
Does not cause headache.
Not the mechanism of overuse headache.
Paracetamol at these doses does not cause the headache.

steps.x: B: Gradual normalisation of central pain pathways. Overuse headache settles over weeks as central pain pathways normalise.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman has had bilateral pressing headaches on more than 15 days a month for 2 years. She does not overuse analgesia. Her scalp feels sore when brushing her hair and light pressure over many muscles is painful. ESR and CRP are normal. Her BP is 126/78 mmHg and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for her chronic headache?
o: Giant cell inflammation of the temporal artery
Vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root
questions.e: Tension-type headache arises from peripheral myofascial mechanisms (pericranial muscle tenderness) combined with central sensitisation of pain pathways, which explains widespread tenderness in chronic cases.

clues: light pressure over many muscles is painful
steps.x: Chronic bilateral pressing headache, widespread tenderness, normal inflammatory markers, no overuse.

elim: Causes migraine aura.
ESR and CRP are normal.
She does not overuse analgesia.
Causes trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.x: C: Myofascial tenderness with central sensitisation. Tension-type headache: peripheral myofascial plus central sensitisation.
